short_title: Kamera World Inc. v. Reddot Imaging Philippines, Inc.
full_title: KAMERA WORLD INC., PETITIONER, VS. REDDOT IMAGING PHILIPPINES, INC., RESPONDENT.
subject: Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds
syllabus_topic: VIII. Obligations and Contracts > A. Obligations > 5. Extinguishment > a. Payment or Performance
topics: Dacion en pago as a special mode of payment that partakes of a sale
Essential requisites of a contract (Art. 1318, Civil Code)
Perfection not undone by a later term sheet that is a mere recommended addendum
Estoppel against questioning the consideration after acknowledging it in writing
Rule 45: authority of corporate signatories is a question of fact

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: III. Civil Procedure > S. Post-judgment Remedies > 5. Appeal and Review > e. Modes > v. Appeal by Certiorari to SC (Rule 45)

doctrine:
**Dacion en pago** is the transmission of the ownership of a thing by the debtor to the creditor as an accepted equivalent of the performance of an obligation. It partakes of the nature of a sale: the creditor is really buying the debtor's property, payment for which is charged against the debt. Hence the essential requisites of a contract under **Art. 1318 of the Civil Code** (consent, object certain, and cause) must be present, **except that the consideration or purchase price is deemed to be the existing debt**; in its modern concept it is an objective novation (reiterating *Dacquel v. Spouses Sotelo*). A sale is perfected upon the meeting of minds on the object and the price.

**A memorandum of agreement signed by both parties' representatives, identifying the property and fixing the price to be applied against the debtor's obligations, is a perfected, binding contract.** Later e-mails and a term sheet proposing revisions do not undo perfection where they do not change, amend, revise or deviate from the purpose of the agreement; they are at most a recommended addendum.

A party that acknowledged in writing that the down payment it received included the credits of a related company is **estopped** from later claiming that the consideration was defective for including those credits. Whether the corporate signatories were authorized by board resolutions is a **question of fact** not reviewable under Rule 45, and a party seeking relaxation of that rule must prove an exceptionally meritorious reason.
facts:
In 2008, I-Digiworld, Inc. delivered imaging equipment and camera products to Kameraworld Inc. for sale in its outlets, with Kameraworld to remit the proceeds less its margin. Kameraworld failed to remit, and its payables reached PHP 12,000,000.00. In 2011, to settle, Kameraworld and I-Digiworld signed a deed of sale over a Kameraworld condominium unit, but I-Digiworld, through its president Dennie T. Dy, instead proposed to buy Kameraworld's properties in España, Sampaloc, Manila (TCT Nos. 131996 and 131997) for PHP 32,500,000.00. Dy said I-Digiworld would assign its right to collect the PHP 12,000,000.00 to Reddot Imaging Philippines, Inc., which had the same directors.

The España properties were mortgaged to BPI, as Kameraworld disclosed. With Kameraworld's consent, Reddot entered the premises, introduced improvements, and paid upkeep and realty taxes. In September 2012, Reddot issued three checks to Kameraworld for PHP 7,500,000.00, PHP 1,500,000.00 and PHP 1,000,000.00. Further checks were suspended after a BIR tax lien on the properties surfaced and Chinabank disapproved Reddot's loan.

On July 10, 2013, Kameraworld's chairperson, Ma. Teresa Alba, acknowledged receipt of a PHP 1,500,000.00 check as "additional downpayment" on the España property, to be used to settle the tax lien, and stated a total down payment of PHP 15,289,897.00, consisting of the "[o]utstanding payable to I-Digiworld/Reddot Imaging Philippines" of PHP 13,789,897.70 plus the new check. The same day, Kameraworld (through its president John Pacific Castro) and Reddot (through Dy) signed a Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) under which Kameraworld offered the España properties as payment of its obligation for a total consideration of PHP 32,500,000.00. Reddot would pay the PHP 10,000,000.00 release value of the BPI mortgage and pay the remaining balance of PHP 7,931,345.37 once the BIR lifted the tax lien.

In 2014, Reddot sent a draft deed of sale, to which Castro was noncommittal. In August 2014, Reddot sent Kameraworld checks payable to BPI for PHP 10,000,000.00 and PHP 721,243.07 and undertook to pay the balance within five days after the tax lien was removed. Alba replied that the MOA was only a proposal because she had not signed it, and Kameraworld pointed to a later term sheet with improved terms, which it rejected. Reddot sued for specific performance. The RTC held the MOA binding; the CA affirmed with modifications, characterizing the MOA as a dacion en pago governed by the law on sales.
issues: Whether the alleged lack of board authority of the signatories to the MOA may be reviewed in a Rule 45 petition.
Whether the MOA is a valid contract (a dacion en pago) despite Kameraworld's claims of defective consent and consideration.
Whether the later e-mails and term sheet show that there was no meeting of the minds, so that the MOA was never perfected.
ruling:
**1. No.** Only questions of law may be raised in a Rule 45 petition. Whether board resolutions authorized Dy and Castro to sign for their corporations is a question of fact. Kameraworld cited the recognized exceptions but failed to establish which of them applied. Those who seek exemption from a procedural rule bear the burden of proving an exceptionally meritorious reason (*Waterfront Cebu City Casino Hotel, Inc. v. Ledesma*).

**2. Yes.** A contract requires consent, object certain, and cause (Art. 1318), and a sale is perfected upon the meeting of minds on the thing and the price (*Heirs of Dr. Mario S. Intac v. CA*). The MOA had consent (the signatures of Castro and Dy), an object certain (the España properties), and a cause (the PHP 32,500,000.00 price). Under *Dacquel v. Spouses Sotelo*, dacion en pago is the transmission of ownership of a thing by the debtor to the creditor as an accepted equivalent of performance; it partakes of a sale and requires the elements of a contract of sale, except that the consideration is deemed to be the existing debt. On the alleged defect in consideration because it included I-Digiworld's credits, **Kameraworld was estopped**: in the July 10, 2013 letter, Alba acknowledged the PHP 1,500,000.00 down payment and a total of PHP 15,289,897.00 received, of which PHP 13,789,897.00 represented Kameraworld's payables not only to Reddot but also to I-Digiworld.

**3. No.** The MOA was perfected because all the requisites of a valid contract concurred. The Court agreed with the RTC that the term sheet could be deemed "only as a recommended addendum" to the MOA, since it did not change, amend, revise or deviate from the purpose for which the MOA was created; it could not affect the validity of a complete agreement. The CA committed no reversible error, and the Court adopted the CA's dispositive portion as "spot on" in fixing the parties' obligations and remedies.
disposition: The petition was DENIED, and the CA Decision dated February 28, 2019 and Resolution dated July 5, 2019 in CA-G.R. CV No. 109047 were AFFIRMED. As affirmed, the CA judgment: declared the MOA a valid and binding contract; required BPI to accept Reddot's tender of payment of Kameraworld's loan and release the owner's duplicate titles to Reddot; ordered Kameraworld to cause the lifting of the tax lien within 30 days from finality, failing which Reddot may do so at Kameraworld's expense and pay whatever balance of the price remains after deducting the cost; ordered Kameraworld to execute a deed of absolute sale upon delivery of the balance (PHP 7,931,345.37 if Kameraworld settles the tax lien, or the remainder after deducting its cost); dismissed Kameraworld's counterclaims; and deleted the RTC's awards of moral and temperate damages and attorney's fees.

bar_questions.q: Delta Corp. owed Echo Corp. PHP 20,000,000.00 for unpaid deliveries. Their presidents signed a memorandum of agreement in which Delta offered its warehouse in payment of its debt for a total consideration of PHP 30,000,000.00; the debt would be credited against the price, and Echo would pay the PHP 10,000,000.00 difference once Delta cleared a tax lien on the property. Later, Delta's chairperson refused to execute a deed of sale, claiming that the MOA was a mere proposal because she did not sign it. (a) What is the nature of the MOA? (b) Is it a binding contract?

alac.answer: (a) It is a dacion en pago. (b) Yes, it is a perfected and binding contract.
alac.legal_basis: Dacion en pago is the transmission of the ownership of a thing by the debtor to the creditor as an accepted equivalent of the performance of an obligation. It partakes of the nature of a sale, so the essential requisites of a contract under Art. 1318 of the Civil Code (consent, object certain, and cause) must be present, with the existing debt deemed the consideration or purchase price. An MOA signed by both parties' representatives that identifies the property and fixes the price is a valid contract of this kind (Kamera World Inc. v. Reddot Imaging Philippines, Inc., G.R. No. 248256, April 17, 2023, citing Dacquel v. Spouses Sotelo).
alac.application: Delta, the debtor, offered its warehouse and Echo, the creditor, accepted it as payment of the debt, with the excess of the price payable in cash. This is a dacion en pago. Consent is shown by the signatures of both presidents; the object is the warehouse; the cause is the PHP 30,000,000.00 price, against which the existing debt is credited. The chairperson's failure to sign does not negate consent, because Delta signed through its president; any claim that he lacked authority is a factual matter that Delta must prove at trial.
alac.conclusion: The MOA is a perfected dacion en pago that binds Delta.

bar_questions.q: Same facts. Delta further argues that (a) after the MOA was signed, Echo sent a term sheet proposing additional details on the payment schedule and closing documents, which Delta rejected, so the term sheet was a counter-offer showing that there was no meeting of the minds; and (b) the consideration is defective because PHP 5,000,000.00 of the debt credited under the MOA was owed not to Echo but to Foxtrot Corp., Echo's sister company, which is not a party to the MOA. The evidence shows that on the day the MOA was signed, Delta's chairperson signed a receipt acknowledging a down payment and stating that the total credited included the outstanding payable to "Echo/Foxtrot." Rule on both arguments.

alac.answer: Both arguments fail. (a) The term sheet did not undo the perfected MOA. (b) Delta is estopped from questioning the inclusion of Foxtrot's credit in the consideration.
alac.legal_basis: In Kamera World Inc. v. Reddot Imaging Philippines, Inc. (G.R. No. 248256, April 17, 2023), the Court held that a later term sheet that did not change, amend, revise or deviate from the purpose of a complete MOA was only a recommended addendum and could not affect the validity of the perfected contract. It also held the debtor estopped from claiming that the consideration was defective for including the credits of the creditor's affiliate, because its chairperson had acknowledged in writing that the down payment and the total amount received included payables to both companies.
alac.application: (a) The MOA already contained all the requisites of a valid contract: the parties' consent, the warehouse, and the price. Echo's term sheet only proposed details on payment schedule and documents without altering the object, the price or the purpose of the MOA, so it was a mere recommended addendum and not a counter-offer that prevented perfection. (b) Delta's own chairperson acknowledged, on the day the MOA was signed, that the amounts credited included the payable to "Echo/Foxtrot." Having represented that Foxtrot's credit formed part of the consideration, Delta cannot now deny it to escape the contract.
alac.conclusion: The MOA remains a perfected and binding dacion en pago, and Delta must comply with it.

bar_questions.q: After losing in the RTC and the CA, Delta files a Rule 45 petition before the Supreme Court, arguing that the MOA is void for lack of consent because no board resolution authorized its president to sign it. Delta enumerates the recognized exceptions to the rule that only questions of law may be raised, but does not show which exception applies. Will the Supreme Court review this issue?

alac.answer: No. Whether the signatory was authorized by a board resolution is a question of fact that the Supreme Court will not review under Rule 45, and Delta has not shown that an exception applies.
alac.legal_basis: In a petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45 of the Rules of Court, only questions of law may be raised. The presence or absence of board resolutions authorizing the signatories of an agreement is a question of fact. A party that merely cites the exceptions without clearly establishing which one applies is not entitled to relaxation, because those who seek exemption from a procedural rule bear the burden of proving an exceptionally meritorious reason (Kamera World Inc. v. Reddot Imaging Philippines, Inc., G.R. No. 248256, April 17, 2023, citing Waterfront Cebu City Casino Hotel, Inc. v. Ledesma).
alac.application: Delta's argument would require the Court to determine from the evidence whether a board resolution existed and whether its president was in fact authorized. That is a factual matter for the trial court, already passed upon below. Listing the exceptions without demonstrating that one fits the case does not discharge Delta's burden to justify a departure from the rule.
alac.conclusion: The Supreme Court will not review the alleged lack of board authority, and the finding of consent stands.

notes: The decision quotes the RTC as citing "Article 218" of the Civil Code for the requisites of a contract; the provision is Art. 1318, which the Supreme Court itself quotes. Figures in the quoted documents vary slightly: the MOA states the receivable as PHP 15,289,897.70 in its whereas clause and PHP 15,298,897.70 in its computation, Alba's receipt totals PHP 15,289,897.00, and the check number appears as both 255015 and 225015. The digest uses the figures as the Court states them. The caption reads "Kamera World Inc." while the body uses "Kameraworld." The Supreme Court did not itself discuss Art. 1191; the CA's reliance on it is carried only through the adopted dispositive portion.
